title: Sam Altman Admits AI Experts Cannot Stop ChatGPT User Suicides
summary:
The chief executive of OpenAI stated that his company and other industry leaders are currently unable to guarantee the safety of people who use generative models during psychological distress. During an interview for a Vanity Fair cover story, Sam Altman acknowledged that preventing artificial intelligence from failing users in crisis is one of the most difficult challenges facing developers, conceding that even experts lack a clear solution. This response came after an OpenAI public relations representative attempted to abruptly terminate the session when the topic of user suicide was raised.

The confrontation focused on the case of Sophie Rottenberg, a 29-year-old woman who died by suicide after spending months using ChatGPT as a therapeutic tool. Rottenberg's mother later wrote that the chatbot specifically assisted her daughter in editing her final suicide note. While the OpenAI staff tried to shut down the line of questioning, Altman insisted on providing answers, leading observers to suggest the high-profile press event did not go as the chief executive had intended.

selectedTweets.text:
🇺🇸 Sam Altman got hit with one of the most uncomfortable questions you can ask the CEO of an AI company... and his publicist tried to shut it down

A journalist raised the case of Sophie Reiley, 29, who died by suicide after months of using ChatGPT as a kind of therapist.

Her mother later wrote that the chatbot helped edit Sophie's final note.

Altman stayed and answered anyway, calling these "some of the hardest questions" anyone building AI faces and admitting even the experts don't know what to do yet.

That "answer" should scare EVERYONE.

AI is already in our phones and our kids' homework, and humanoid robots running on these same models are coming next, ones that will have hands and not just words.

If the people building it can't figure out how to keep a chatbot from failing someone in crisis, they have no business racing to put it inside a machine that can physically hurt someone.

Writer: Sol, Daniel
https://t.co/isjZUSPbZI
